description: JT_1 is a team comprising of 6 members from the A Level Institution LGS JT with interests in environmental engineering and machine learning
summary:
We developed an interactive program, a tool which helps farmers test crop rotations before planting, and others to plan and pick suitable land, called Agrorithm. . A farmer enters their field, water supply, soil and current crops. Agrorithm compares that plan with alternatives over three years and marks any option that breaks basic rules, such as sowing dates, markets or water limits.
Agrorithm faces the presented case in light of NASA’s data to produce usable and direct decisions. NASA POWER weather drives a water-balance estimate for each rotation, and NASA/USGS satellite imagery provides a cloud-filtered vegetation history. Farmers can simulate their planned crops inlight of varying conditions, testing and pre planning any and all issues ie rain or hotter weather, view 3D soil and groundwater visuals,  and save progress locally, and export a transparent PDF report. Why this matters? Well Pakistan faces changing climate, water pressure and growing population, whose needs are not sufficiently met and areas are rendered unusable due to the lack of knowledge possessed by farmers. Agrorithm helps farmers plan around water, helping to conserve the resources and use them as efficiently as possible.
details: In light of the drastically changing environment and the growing population of Pakistan, out of which 16.1% is malnourished due to the increasing food prices caused by the lack of utilization of land as well as the inefficiencies accompanying it, team Jt_1 has presented the Program Agrorithm. Agrorithm provides an interactive platform that helps farmers in Punjab adapt their crop rotations using NASA data. Users begin with a guided field setup covering location, area, irrigation method and efficiency, water limits, soil properties, equipment, market access, budget, crop exclusions and their current rotation. Agrorithm then compares their existing data against alternative rotations over a common 36-month period, such as adding a mungbean pulse or a living cover crop. The platform is powered by two NASA datasets. NASA POWER daily weather (2018–2024) drives a root-zone water balance based on Hargreaves evapotranspiration and FAO-56 crop coefficients Each dataset input by the user is judged on various field factors, including delivered irrigation water, live cover, residue-only days, crop diversity, legume inclusion and heat or frost exposure These recommendations are also checked against hard feasibility rules for sowing windows, transition buffers, equipment, markets and water limits. Users can also stress-test results by changing rainfall, temperature, water budget and crop-coefficient assumptions based on changing weather patterns, expected changes and based on that learn ways to overcome said problems more efficiently and better. A historical replay and a 6 case sensitivity check then show how stable the comparison is. Every input, assumption, crop parameter and data limit is carried into a transparent PDF report. In order to show creativity and easy visualization, we also used Blender 5.2 to model some plants and crops, and took inspiration from websites such as Lusion in order to make our own website interactive and easy to navigate.
dataRefs: NASA POWER — historical daily temperature and precipitation
NASA MERRA-2 — reanalysis underlying POWER meteorology
NASA/USGS HLS L30 v2.0 — vegetation observations
NASA Blue Marble: Next Generation — atlas imagery
NASA Earth with Clouds — 3D Earth presentation asset
